subject: biology
title: Stem cells
summary: What stem cells are, how their potency ranges from totipotent to unipotent, how embryonic, adult and induced pluripotent stem cells differ, and how they are used in medicine along with the ethical issues involved.
body:
You began as a single cell, yet your body now has hundreds of different kinds of cells, from nerve cells to red blood cells. Stem cells are the unspecialised cells that make this possible, and they keep working throughout life to repair and replace tissues. Because they can become other cell types, stem cells are also at the centre of some of the most exciting, and debated, areas of modern medicine.

## Key ideas

### What is a stem cell?

A **stem cell** is an unspecialised cell with two special properties:

1. **Self-renewal**: it can divide by mitosis many times to make more stem cells.
2. **Differentiation**: it can develop into one or more specialised cell types.

When a stem cell divides, the daughter cells can either stay as stem cells or begin to specialise. This lets the body keep a supply of stem cells while also producing new working cells.

### Differentiation

**Differentiation** is the process by which an unspecialised cell becomes a specialised cell with a particular structure and function, such as a muscle cell full of contractile proteins or a red blood cell packed with haemoglobin.

Almost every cell in your body has the same DNA. Cells become different because they **express** (switch on) different genes. A muscle cell switches on the genes for muscle proteins and switches off many others. Signals from neighbouring cells and the cell's surroundings help decide which genes are switched on. Once a cell is fully differentiated it usually cannot change into a different type, and many differentiated cells stop dividing.

### Potency: how many cell types can a stem cell become?

**Potency** describes how many different cell types a stem cell can give rise to. As development goes on, potency usually narrows.

| Potency | Can become | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Totipotent** | Every cell type, including the placenta and other tissues that support the embryo; can form a whole organism | The zygote (fertilised egg) and cells of the first few divisions |
| **Pluripotent** | Any cell type of the body, but not the placenta and supporting tissues; cannot form a whole organism alone | Cells of the inner cell mass of a blastocyst (an early embryo of around 5 days) |
| **Multipotent** | Several cell types within one related family | Blood stem cells in bone marrow, which make red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets |
| **Unipotent** | Only one cell type (but can still self-renew) | Skin stem cells that make one kind of skin cell |

A way to remember: 'toti' means 'all', 'pluri' means 'many', 'multi' means 'several', and 'uni' means 'one'.

### Embryonic stem cells

**Embryonic stem cells** are taken from the inner cell mass of a **blastocyst**, a hollow ball of cells formed a few days after fertilisation. Embryos used are often spare ones left over from IVF treatment, donated with consent.

- Advantages: they are pluripotent, so they could make almost any cell type; they divide readily in the laboratory.
- Disadvantages: collecting them destroys the embryo, which raises ethical concerns; cells from a donor embryo are not genetically matched to the patient, so they may be **rejected** by the immune system; they may form tumours if their division is not controlled.

### Adult (somatic) stem cells

**Adult stem cells** (also called somatic stem cells) are found in small numbers in many tissues of children and adults, such as bone marrow, skin, the gut lining and fat. Their job is to replace cells that wear out or are damaged. Stem cells from umbilical cord blood are similar and are collected at birth.

- Advantages: no embryo is destroyed; a patient's own cells can be used, so there is no risk of rejection.
- Disadvantages: they are usually multipotent or unipotent, so they make a narrower range of cells; they are rare and can be hard to find, collect and grow.

### Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells)

**Induced pluripotent stem cells** are ordinary differentiated adult cells, such as skin cells, that have been reprogrammed in the laboratory to become pluripotent again. Scientists add a small number of genes that switch the cell back to an embryonic-like state.

- Advantages: they are pluripotent; no embryo is needed; they can be made from the patient's own cells, so rejection is much less likely. They also let researchers grow a patient's own diseased cells in a dish to study a disease and test drugs.
- Disadvantages: the reprogramming process can cause genetic changes, and there is a risk of tumours; making them is slow and expensive.

### Medical uses

- **Bone marrow transplants** (blood stem cell transplants) are an established treatment for leukaemia and some other blood disorders. Healthy blood stem cells replace the patient's diseased bone marrow.
- **Skin grafts** grown from a patient's own skin stem cells can be used to treat severe burns.
- **Research** into replacing damaged cells in conditions such as spinal cord injury, type 1 diabetes and Parkinson's disease. Most of these uses are still being tested in clinical trials rather than being routine treatments.
- **Drug testing and disease modelling** using specialised cells grown from stem cells.

### Ethical issues

Stem cell research raises questions on which people disagree.

- **Status of the embryo**: some people believe an embryo has the same moral value as a person from fertilisation, so destroying one to collect stem cells is wrong. Others believe the possible benefit to many patients outweighs the use of an early embryo that would otherwise be discarded.
- **Consent**: donors of embryos, eggs or tissue must give informed consent.
- **Safety**: untested treatments could cause tumours or other harm. Some clinics around the world sell unproven 'stem cell therapies', which can be dangerous.
- **Access and cost**: new treatments may be expensive, raising questions about who can use them.

In Australia, research on human embryos is regulated by law and requires a licence. iPS cells and adult stem cells avoid the main embryo issue, which is one reason they are so widely researched.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Classifying potency

A cell taken from bone marrow can form red blood cells, several types of white blood cells and platelets, but not nerve or muscle cells. What is its potency?

Step 1. It can make more than one cell type, so it is not unipotent.

Step 2. All its products belong to one family (blood cells); it cannot make unrelated types such as nerve cells, so it is not pluripotent.

Step 3. Conclusion: it is multipotent.

### Example 2: Choosing a stem cell source

A patient needs new insulin-making cells. Doctors consider (a) embryonic stem cells from a donated embryo or (b) iPS cells made from the patient's skin.

Step 1. Both types are pluripotent, so both could in principle form insulin-making cells.

Step 2. Rejection: embryonic stem cells come from a different individual, so the patient's immune system may attack them. iPS cells are genetically identical to the patient, so rejection is far less likely.

Step 3. Ethics: embryonic stem cells require destroying an embryo; iPS cells do not.

Step 4. Risks to mention: both could form tumours if not fully controlled, and iPS reprogramming may introduce genetic changes.

Conclusion: iPS cells avoid rejection and the embryo issue, but safety would need careful testing.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing up totipotent and pluripotent. Only totipotent cells can make the placenta and supporting tissues and therefore a whole organism.
- Thinking differentiated cells have different DNA. They have the same DNA but express different genes.
- Saying adult stem cells are only found in adults. They are found in children too; 'adult' just means 'not embryonic'.
- Saying iPS cells come from embryos. They are made from ordinary body cells.
- Presenting ethical issues as having one correct answer. Show that you understand the different viewpoints.

## Exam tips

- Learn the four potency terms with a clear example of each; questions often ask you to classify a described cell.
- Comparison questions (embryonic vs adult vs iPS) reward matched points on potency, source, rejection risk and ethics.
- For ethics questions, state an issue, explain the different views, and link to a specific type of stem cell. Avoid vague statements such as 'it's wrong'.
- Link differentiation to gene expression to show deeper understanding.

## Key terms

- **Stem cell** — an unspecialised cell that can self-renew and differentiate into specialised cells.
- **Differentiation** — the process by which a cell becomes specialised by expressing particular genes.
- **Potency** — the range of cell types a stem cell can become.
- **Totipotent** — able to form all cell types, including supporting tissues such as the placenta.
- **Pluripotent** — able to form any cell type of the body but not supporting tissues.
- **Multipotent** — able to form a limited range of related cell types.
- **Unipotent** — able to form only one cell type.
- **Blastocyst** — an early embryo, a hollow ball of cells containing the inner cell mass.
- **Adult (somatic) stem cell** — a stem cell found in a tissue after birth that replaces cells in that tissue.
- **Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPS cell)** — a body cell reprogrammed in the laboratory to become pluripotent.
- **Rejection** — an immune attack on transplanted cells recognised as foreign.

## Summary

- Stem cells can self-renew and differentiate into specialised cells.
- Differentiation happens by switching different genes on and off; the DNA stays the same.
- Potency narrows from totipotent (zygote) to pluripotent (inner cell mass) to multipotent (bone marrow) to unipotent.
- Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent but raise ethical and rejection issues; adult stem cells avoid these but are less flexible.
- iPS cells are reprogrammed body cells: pluripotent, patient-matched, but with safety concerns.
- Bone marrow transplants are an established use; many other therapies are still being researched.

options.A: A cell from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst
options.B: A blood stem cell in bone marrow

questions.explanation: The zygote can form every cell type, including the placenta, so it is totipotent. A is tempting because inner cell mass cells are very flexible, but they are pluripotent: they cannot form the placenta and supporting tissues.

questions.prompt: Which two properties together define a stem cell?

options.A: It is specialised and can no longer divide.
options.B: It can self-renew and can differentiate into specialised cells.
options.C: It has different DNA from other cells and can divide by meiosis.
options.D: It is only found in embryos and can form a whole organism.

questions.explanation: Stem cells make more stem cells (self-renewal) and can become specialised cells (differentiation). D is tempting but wrong: adult stem cells exist after birth, and most stem cells cannot form a whole organism.

questions.prompt: Muscle cells and nerve cells from the same person look and work very differently. The best explanation is that

options.B: nerve cells have lost some of their chromosomes.
options.D: they contain the same genes but express different genes.

questions.explanation: Almost all body cells carry the same DNA; differentiation depends on which genes are switched on. A is the tempting misconception, but both cells came from the same zygote by mitosis, which copies DNA exactly.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells?

options.A: They are adult body cells reprogrammed in the laboratory to become pluripotent.
options.B: They are collected from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst.
options.C: They are multipotent cells found in umbilical cord blood.
options.D: They are totipotent cells that can form a whole organism.

questions.explanation: iPS cells are made by reprogramming differentiated body cells, such as skin cells, back to a pluripotent state. B describes embryonic stem cells, which is the tempting confusion because both are pluripotent.

questions.prompt: A major advantage of using a patient's own adult stem cells rather than donor embryonic stem cells is that

options.A: adult stem cells can form more cell types.
options.B: adult stem cells divide faster in the laboratory.
options.C: the cells are genetically matched to the patient, so the risk of immune rejection is very low.

questions.explanation: The patient's own cells will not be recognised as foreign, so rejection is unlikely, and no embryo is destroyed. A is the reverse of the truth: embryonic stem cells are pluripotent and can form more cell types than multipotent adult stem cells.

questions.prompt: A stem cell found in the lining of the gut can produce four types of gut lining cells but cannot produce blood, nerve or muscle cells. This stem cell is
questions.explanation: It makes several related cell types within one tissue, so it is multipotent. D is tempting because it is limited to one tissue, but unipotent cells make only one cell type, and this cell makes four.

questions.prompt: A patient with leukaemia has their diseased bone marrow destroyed and then receives blood stem cells from a matched donor. The new stem cells are useful because they

options.A: can develop into all the types of blood cells the patient needs.
options.B: will form a new placenta to support the patient.
options.C: are totipotent and will form new organs.
options.D: will stop dividing once inside the patient.

questions.explanation: Blood stem cells are multipotent: they self-renew and make red cells, white cells and platelets, rebuilding the patient's blood supply. C is tempting because stem cells sound all-powerful, but bone marrow stem cells are multipotent, not totipotent.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the main ethical objection to embryonic stem cell research?

options.A: Embryonic stem cells cannot differentiate, so research wastes money.
options.B: Using iPS cells requires destroying embryos.
options.C: Embryonic stem cells always cause tumours.
options.D: Collecting the cells destroys the embryo, which some people believe has the moral status of a person.

questions.explanation: The main objection is that taking the inner cell mass destroys an embryo, which some people view as a human life. B is tempting because iPS cells are part of the same debate, but iPS cells are made from body cells and need no embryo; that is their main ethical advantage.
